criteria.criterion: In crates/athena-core/src/status/throughput.rs, landing_record_time selects the earliest (.min()) created_at among landings/ records carrying the job's job_landing commit, and its doc comment says earliest.
criteria.evidence: I read throughput.rs lines 389-404. The function filters on LandingKind::JobLanding with the job's id, maps to created_at and calls `.min()`. The doc comment says "the earliest `landings/` record" and explains that on a stacked branch later landings carry earlier jobs' commits.

criteria.criterion: A new unit test in crates/athena-core/src/status/throughput.rs (or its tests module) builds a fixture where one job's commit is carried by two landing records and asserts landing_end equals the first record's time, not the second.
criteria.evidence: The test `the_landing_stage_ends_at_the_first_of_two_landing_records_carrying_the_commit` is in status.rs `planning_cost_tests`, the module that holds the throughput tests. It adds two landing records for LANDED_JOB, 2026-10-30T10:23Z listed first and 2026-10-29T10:23Z second, and asserts landing_and_rebuild == 6.0 min, which is the end at the earlier record. Under the old `.max()` the stage would end at the later record, about 1,446 min, so the test fails without the fix. It passed in my run.

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p athena-core` : the new fixture test and all existing tests pass.
criteria.evidence: My filtered run passed 61 of 61, including the new test and the three neighbouring landing-stage tests. Athena's recorded full-suite run, `cargo test --locked` (CI run 43571069667 for 6b6736ff), passed.

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo run -p athena-cli -- status --snapshot <records directory>` on the real records: for jobs npqp, pg2d, yp1e, abbg and 4z98 the landing duration printed is within 15 minutes of the outcome-to-main-push gap, the expected range being 5 to 12 minutes after the landed outcome (up to 27 minutes tolerance) taken from main-branch commit times in git log, an independent source the change does not compute; the landing median is far below 1,327.8 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Status on the evidence snapshot printed "landing and rebuild 14.8" as the median over the last 20 measured jobs, far below 1,327.8. Status prints only medians, not per-job durations, so I worked out each job's stage from the snapshot records. Stage end is the earliest landing record carrying the job's commit; stage start is the verifier's end, about 3 s before the outcome. For comparison I took the main commit time of each earliest landing's host_commit from history.json. Results, in minutes after the outcome (stage / main commit): 4z98 6.7 / 5.6, abbg 12.6 / 11.4, yp1e 7.5 / 6.2, pg2d 6.9 / 5.6, npqp 6.9 / 5.7. Each stage is within about 1.3 min of the main-commit gap, well inside the 15-minute tolerance. All of this reads the read-only evidence snapshot, not the working copy.

criteria.criterion: CHANGELOG.md has an entry stating the old landing median (1,327.8 minutes as reported, or as measured before) and the new landing median measured after the change, and that landing figures use the earliest landing record.
criteria.evidence: A new entry under Fixed gives the old median as 2896.0 min, measured at base, and notes the review reported 1,327.8 min. It gives the new median as 14.8 min and says the stage now ends at the earliest landing record. My status run reproduced 14.8. I did not reproduce 2896.0, because building the base tree would change git state. The 1,327.8 figure does appear in throughput review 20261107-224336-2v6c in the snapshot.

summary: The change does what was asked: the "landing and rebuild" stage now ends at the earliest landing record that carries the job's commit, not the newest. The code change is one call, `.max()` to `.min()` in landing_record_time, plus an updated doc comment. That approach is sound: the first landing that carries a commit is the one that merged it. A new fixture test lists the later record first and passes only with the fix. On the real records snapshot, `athena status` now prints a landing median of 14.8 min; the review reported 1,327.8. Status prints only medians, so I checked the five named jobs from the records. Their stages run 6.7 to 12.6 min from the landed outcome, each within about 1.3 min of the main commit time in history.json and inside the 5 to 12 minute window. My targeted athena-core tests passed, and Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and test checks passed. Two small notes, neither blocking: the test was added to status.rs, which is on the deliverables list, and I could not reproduce the changelog's old median of 2896.0 min, because measuring the base would change git state.
